latest_rss.title: AI Lessons From Russia’s War in Ukraine
latest_rss.summary:
Executive Summary:




Chinese military writers studying the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Russia’s war in Ukraine have concluded that its decisive value lies in shortening the kill chain rather than in fully autonomous weapons.



In their reading, AI plays four roles: turning sensor data into targets, accelerating planning and command, keeping drones on target when jamming cuts the link, and mass-produced propaganda and deep-fakes.



Each of these roles rests on the combat data, computing power, chips, and AI models that the PRC wishes to control domestically. Starlink’s wartime restrictions and Russia’s reliance on U.S. chips serve as warnings.



The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is turning these lessons into AI planning systems, unmanned units, and procurement of domestic large language models (LLMs). Some concede that PLA’s AI is still used mainly for auxiliary tasks, with these authors acknowledging that doctrine lags technological advancements.

latest_rss.summary: The high seas have always come with high stakes – and for all the living things in the water, these couldn't be higher.The vast two-thirds of the ocean beyond national jurisdiction has been hit by overfishing, shipping traffic and plastic pollution, while emerging threats like deep-sea mining and marine carbon dioxide removal proposals loom on the horizon. Although already subject to international law, there was no global framework to protect these waters. With the UN High Seas Treaty (formally known as the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction, or BBNJ, Agreement) entering into force on January 17, 2026, a new legal framework for conserving and sustainably using marine biodiversity in these shared waters is in place.At the UN biodiversity summit (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, this week, experts met to figure out how different global rules can work together to save the ocean.The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is the broad framework for biodiversity conservation. latest_rss.summary:
China has accused the Philippines of setting up “numerous obstacles” to attending a meeting with defence ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and of violating “basic diplomatic protocols”.
The row, which follows years of tension over the two countries’ competing claims to the South China Sea, saw Beijing sending its defence attache to the meeting in the Philippines – the lowest-ranking Chinese representative at the event since it was first held in 2010.
